newsitem.title: USA: Aviron stock up after flu treatment reported effective.
newsitem.headline: Aviron stock up after flu treatment reported effective.

text.p: Aviron stock surged 28 percent Monday after the government reported a nasal spray vaccine licensed by the biopharmaceutical company proved very effective in preventing flu among young children in a clinical trial.
Aviron stock climbed $3.75 to $17.125 on Nasdaq, where it was the ninth-biggest percentage gainer.

The vaccine, developed by government and university scientists over 30 years, could be in use by fall 1999 under the licensing agreement with the Mountain View, Calif.-based company, the National Institutes of Health said.

Aviron will ask the federal Food and Drug Administration next year to approve use of the vaccine in children and healthy adults and intends to make it available by prescription for the fall 1999 flu season, NIH said.

In the trial conducted last year, only 1 percent of 1,070 children who received the vaccine developed confirmed influenza, compared with 18 percent of children who received a placebo, NIH said in a statement.
"The initial results from this trial are very exciting," said Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institutes of Health's National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

"An influenza vaccine given in a nasal spray would be easier to administer and more acceptable than an injection, especially to children. Such a vaccine could have a significant impact on public health," he said.
As with injected flu vaccine, the nasal vaccine would be needed annually, because virus strains change from year to year.

Each year between 35 million and 50 million Americans get flu, and more than 20,000 people die, NIH said. In addition to the cost of lost workdays, an estimated $4.6 billion is spent annually on direct medical costs.
